Common Causes: Sharp object, fall, kitchen accident
First Aid Steps: Clean wound, apply pressure to stop bleeding, cover with sterile bandage
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Deep wound, won't stop bleeding, exposed fat/muscle/bone
Male-Specific Notes: Higher incidence in workplace/occupational injuries. Slower wound healing with age
Female-Specific Notes: Similar treatment. Pregnancy affects healing speed. May be more visible scarring concern
When to See a Doctor: Deep, gaping, or won't stop bleeding after 10 min pressure

Common Causes: Fall, friction against rough surface
First Aid Steps: Clean with water, remove debris, apply antiseptic and bandage
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Signs of infection (pus, spreading redness, warmth)
When to See a Doctor: Signs of infection or large/dirty area

Common Causes: Nail, needle, animal bite, splinter
First Aid Steps: Clean thoroughly, do not force out deep objects, cover
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Deep puncture, rusty object, near joint/eye, signs of infection
When to See a Doctor: Any deep puncture (tetanus risk) or from a dirty/rusty object

Common Causes: Blunt impact, fall, bump
First Aid Steps: Ice pack (wrapped) for 15-20 min, rest, elevate if possible
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Rapid severe swelling, inability to move area, numbness
Male-Specific Notes: Common in contact sports. Higher pain tolerance may delay seeking care
Female-Specific Notes: May bruise more easily (genetic/blood clotting factors). Hormonal cycle affects bruising
When to See a Doctor: Severe pain, large swelling, or no improvement after 2 weeks

Common Causes: Twisting/rolling ankle, uneven surface
First Aid Steps: RICE: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Unable to bear weight at all, visible deformity, severe swelling
Male-Specific Notes: Higher incidence in sports. More likely inversion injuries
Female-Specific Notes: Higher ankle sprain rate in women athletes. Hormonal factors (ligament laxity) in luteal phase
When to See a Doctor: Cannot bear weight, severe swelling, or no improvement in a few days

Common Causes: Fall onto outstretched hand, twisting
First Aid Steps: RICE, avoid gripping/lifting with injured wrist
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Visible deformity, severe pain, numbness in fingers
Male-Specific Notes: Often from fall on outstretched hand in sports
Female-Specific Notes: Osteoporosis risk postmenopause increases severity. May be fall-related
When to See a Doctor: Deformity, severe swelling, or persistent pain

Common Causes: Sudden sprinting, inadequate warm-up
First Aid Steps: RICE, gentle stretching once pain subsides
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Sudden 'pop' sensation, inability to walk, large bruising
Male-Specific Notes: Common sports injury. Higher muscle mass aids recovery
Female-Specific Notes: Increased risk mid-cycle due to ligament laxity. Pregnancy affects all muscle strains
When to See a Doctor: Severe pain, inability to walk, or large bruise/swelling

Common Causes: Heavy lifting, sudden twist, poor posture
First Aid Steps: Rest briefly, ice/heat alternating, gentle movement as tolerated
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Numbness/weakness in legs, loss of bladder/bowel control
Male-Specific Notes: Often occupational/lifting. Disc herniation more common
Female-Specific Notes: Pregnancy causes significant strain. Postpartum recovery longer. Osteoporosis risk
When to See a Doctor: Radiating leg pain, numbness, or loss of bladder/bowel control

Common Causes: Fall, direct impact, sports injury
First Aid Steps: Immobilize area, apply cold pack, avoid moving the person unnecessarily
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Visible deformity, bone through skin, severe swelling, numbness
Male-Specific Notes: Higher incidence before age 50. Usually trauma-related
Female-Specific Notes: Osteoporosis risk increases significantly postmenopause. May occur with minimal trauma
When to See a Doctor: Suspected fracture always needs medical imaging/treatment

Common Causes: High-impact trauma, severe fall, accident
First Aid Steps: Do not push bone back in; cover wound with clean cloth; keep still; call emergency services
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Bone visible through skin, heavy bleeding, shock symptoms
Male-Specific Notes: Usually high-energy trauma (falls, accidents). Faster healing typical
Female-Specific Notes: Similar trauma mechanism. Postmenopausal women at higher risk of complications
When to See a Doctor: Always a medical emergency

Common Causes: Fall on outstretched arm, sports collision
First Aid Steps: Immobilize in position found, do not attempt to relocate it yourself, ice pack
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Visible deformity, numbness/tingling in arm, no pulse in limb
Male-Specific Notes: Higher incidence in contact sports. Faster typical recovery
Female-Specific Notes: Genetic ligament laxity more common. Recurrent dislocations more likely. Slower recovery
When to See a Doctor: Always needs medical relocation and evaluation

Common Causes: Jammed finger, ball sports, fall
First Aid Steps: Immobilize, avoid trying to pop it back yourself, ice pack
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Numbness, severe deformity, no blood flow to fingertip
When to See a Doctor: Any suspected dislocation needs medical evaluation

Common Causes: Fall, sports collision, blow to head
First Aid Steps: Rest, monitor closely, cold pack on area (no swelling relief needed internally)
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Repeated vomiting, worsening headache, confusion, unequal pupils, loss of consciousness
When to See a Doctor: Any head injury with vomiting, confusion, or loss of consciousness — seek care immediately

Common Causes: Car accident, sudden jolt to head/neck
First Aid Steps: Gentle movement as tolerated, ice/heat, OTC pain relief
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Numbness/weakness in arms, severe neck pain, loss of bladder control
When to See a Doctor: Severe pain, numbness, or symptoms worsening after a few days

Common Causes: Brief hot surface/liquid contact, sunburn
First Aid Steps: Cool running water 10-20 min, do not apply ice, loose dressing
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Covers large area, or on face/hands/genitals
When to See a Doctor: Large area, or on sensitive areas (face, hands, groin)

Common Causes: Hot liquid/surface contact, flame, chemical
First Aid Steps: Cool running water, do not pop blisters, cover loosely with sterile non-stick dressing
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Blistering over large area, signs of infection, on face/joints
When to See a Doctor: Blistering, large area, on face/hands/joints, or unclear how deep

Common Causes: Prolonged flame/chemical/electrical contact
First Aid Steps: Call emergency services, cover loosely with clean cloth, do not remove stuck clothing
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Charred/white skin, numbness at site, signs of shock
When to See a Doctor: Always a medical emergency

Common Causes: Prolonged cold exposure, inadequate clothing
First Aid Steps: Move to warmth, warm gradually with lukewarm (not hot) water, do not rub area
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Skin white/waxy and hard, numbness, blistering
When to See a Doctor: Any suspected frostbite needs medical evaluation

Common Causes: Contact with corrosive chemical, splash injury
First Aid Steps: Rinse with large amounts of water for 15-20 min, remove contaminated clothing, call poison control/emergency
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Severe pain, eye involvement, large area affected
When to See a Doctor: Always seek immediate medical attention

Common Causes: Dust/debris, scratch from fingernail or object
First Aid Steps: Do not rub; rinse gently with clean water; blink to encourage tearing
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Object embedded, vision changes, severe pain, chemical involved
When to See a Doctor: Object embedded, vision changes, or pain persists

Common Causes: Dry air, nose picking, minor trauma
First Aid Steps: Sit forward, pinch soft part of nose for 10 minutes, breathe through mouth
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Doesn't stop after 20 min, heavy bleeding, after significant head trauma
When to See a Doctor: Doesn't stop after 20 minutes or is heavy/recurrent

Common Causes: Fall, impact, biting hard object
First Aid Steps: Rinse mouth with warm water, save any tooth fragment, cold compress for swelling
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Severe pain, tooth knocked out completely, visible nerve
When to See a Doctor: Any broken tooth should be seen by a dentist promptly

Common Causes: Mosquito, bee, wasp, ant
First Aid Steps: Remove stinger if present, cold compress, antihistamine/anti-itch cream
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Facial/throat swelling, difficulty breathing, widespread hives (anaphylaxis)
When to See a Doctor: Signs of allergic reaction or infection at site

Common Causes: Dog/cat/wild animal bite or scratch
First Aid Steps: Clean wound thoroughly with soap and water, apply pressure if bleeding, cover
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Deep wound, bite from unknown/wild animal, signs of infection
When to See a Doctor: Always seek care for possible rabies risk and infection/tetanus

Common Causes: Contact with live wire, faulty appliance
First Aid Steps: Turn off power source before touching person; call emergency services; check breathing
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Loss of consciousness, burns, irregular heartbeat, difficulty breathing
When to See a Doctor: Always a medical emergency, even if person seems fine

Common Causes: Friction from shoes/tools, burns
First Aid Steps: Leave intact if possible, cover with padded bandage, avoid popping
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Signs of infection (pus, spreading redness, warmth)
When to See a Doctor: Signs of infection or blister is very large/painful

Common Causes: Sudden twist/pivot in sports, direct blow to knee
First Aid Steps: RICE, avoid weight-bearing, immobilize if possible
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Pop sound at injury, immediate severe swelling, knee gives way
When to See a Doctor: Always needs medical/orthopedic evaluation

Common Causes: Repetitive overhead motion, fall, heavy lifting
First Aid Steps: Rest, ice, avoid overhead activity, gentle range-of-motion as tolerated
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Sudden severe weakness or inability to lift arm at all
When to See a Doctor: Persistent weakness, pain at night, or limited range of motion

Common Causes: Repetitive motion, overtraining, poor technique
First Aid Steps: Rest the area, ice, gradual return to activity, gentle stretching
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Sudden inability to move joint, severe swelling
When to See a Doctor: Persistent pain despite rest, or worsening symptoms

Common Causes: Running on hard surfaces, sudden increase in activity
First Aid Steps: Rest, ice, supportive footwear, gradual return to activity
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Severe localized pain that could indicate stress fracture
When to See a Doctor: Pain persists despite rest or worsens with walking

Common Causes: Prolonged heat exposure, dehydration, overexertion in heat
First Aid Steps: Move to cool area, remove excess clothing, cool with water/fanning, rehydrate
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Confusion, very high body temp, hot dry skin, loss of consciousness (heat stroke)
Typical Recovery Time: Hours to a day for exhaustion
When to See a Doctor: Heat stroke signs (confusion, no sweating, very high temp) is an emergency

Common Causes: Prolonged cold exposure, wet clothing, cold water immersion
First Aid Steps: Move to warmth, remove wet clothing, warm gradually with blankets
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Confusion, slurred speech, slow breathing, loss of consciousness
Typical Recovery Time: Hours to days depending on severity
When to See a Doctor: Moderate-severe hypothermia is a medical emergency

Common Causes: Food/object blocking airway
First Aid Steps: Encourage coughing; if unable to breathe/speak, perform abdominal thrusts (Heimlich)
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Unable to speak/breathe/cough, turning blue, loss of consciousness
When to See a Doctor: Always seek medical check after a choking episode

Common Causes: Submersion in water, swimming accidents
First Aid Steps: Remove from water, call emergency services, begin CPR if not breathing
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Any period of submersion with coughing, breathing difficulty, or altered consciousness
When to See a Doctor: Always requires emergency medical evaluation, even if person seems recovered

Common Causes: Fall from height, diving accident, high-impact collision
First Aid Steps: Do not move the person; keep head/neck still; call emergency services immediately
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Numbness, paralysis, loss of bladder/bowel control, neck/back pain after trauma
Typical Recovery Time: Varies widely, long-term care often needed
When to See a Doctor: Always a medical emergency — do not move the person

Common Causes: Contact with hot surfaces, steam, boiling water, flames
First Aid Steps: Cool with running water for 15-20 mins, remove tight items, cover loosely
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Large area affected, blistering, loss of skin, difficulty breathing
Typical Recovery Time: 1-3 weeks for minor burns; severe burns require hospitalization
Female-Specific Notes: Pregnancy affects pain management options. Healing may be delayed
When to See a Doctor: Burns >2-3 inches, deep, or on face/hands/genitals need medical attention

Common Causes: Falls, motor vehicle accidents, assaults, sports injuries
First Aid Steps: Call 911 for loss of consciousness, monitor breathing, keep person still
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Loss of consciousness, vomiting, clear fluid from ears/nose, confusion
Typical Recovery Time: 2 weeks to months depending on severity; concussion needs medical evaluation
Male-Specific Notes: Higher incidence. May underreport symptoms. Sports-related more common
Female-Specific Notes: Pregnancy complicates imaging/treatment options. Postpartum mood changes post-concussion
When to See a Doctor: ANY significant head trauma requires emergency evaluation

Common Causes: Rolling ankle during sports/walking, stepping off curb, ligament tear
First Aid Steps: Rest, ice (20 mins), compression wrapping, elevation, immobilization
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Severe swelling, inability to bear any weight, visible deformity
Typical Recovery Time: 2-6 weeks for Grade II; 6-12 weeks for Grade III; may need PT
Male-Specific Notes: Higher incidence in male athletes. Faster return-to-play typical
Female-Specific Notes: Hormonal cycle increases injury risk (lower ligament strength mid-cycle). Longer recovery
When to See a Doctor: Cannot bear weight, severe swelling, or no improvement in 48 hours

Common Causes: Cuts from sharp objects, falls, accidents
First Aid Steps: Stop bleeding with pressure, wash with soap/water, apply antibiotic ointment
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Uncontrolled bleeding, gaping wound, deep penetration
Typical Recovery Time: 7-10 days for simple cuts; larger lacerations may need stitches
Male-Specific Notes: Occupational/trauma related. Wound closure easier typically
Female-Specific Notes: Pregnancy affects anesthesia options. Scarring may be cosmetic concern
When to See a Doctor: Deep lacerations, won't stop bleeding, or edges won't stay together

Common Causes: Overexertion, sudden movement, lack of warm-up
First Aid Steps: Rest, ice (15-20 mins), compression, elevation, NSAIDs for pain
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Severe bruising, inability to move muscle, severe pain
Female-Specific Notes: Hormonal effects on muscle recovery. Pregnancy increases strain risk significantly
When to See a Doctor: Severe pain, inability to function, or no improvement in 48 hours

Common Causes: Falls on outstretched arm, contact sports, motor vehicle accidents
First Aid Steps: Immobilize arm with sling, ice, seek immediate medical care
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Severe pain, visible deformity, numbness, unable to move
Typical Recovery Time: 2-4 weeks immobilization; 3-6 months full recovery with PT
Male-Specific Notes: Higher incidence in contact sports. Faster typical recovery
Female-Specific Notes: Genetic ligament laxity more common. Recurrent dislocations more likely. Slower recovery
When to See a Doctor: Always a medical emergency requiring immediate hospital care

Common Causes: Deep wounds, arterial injury, significant trauma
First Aid Steps: Call 911, apply direct pressure with clean cloth, elevate if possible
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Continuous heavy bleeding, blood spurting, dizziness, pale skin
Male-Specific Notes: Consider trauma, alcohol use. Higher baseline hemoglobin
Female-Specific Notes: Pregnancy complicates management. Menstrual bleeding disorders may predispose. Lower baseline Hgb
When to See a Doctor: ALWAYS call 911 for severe bleeding; medical emergency

Common Causes: Prolonged heat exposure, dehydration, intense exercise in heat
First Aid Steps: Move to cool area, remove excess clothing, apply cool water, drink fluids
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: No sweating despite heat, confusion, loss of consciousness, body temp >104°F
Typical Recovery Time: 2-24 hours after cooling and hydration; may need hospital care
Male-Specific Notes: Higher incidence in occupational settings. Sweat response more efficient
Female-Specific Notes: Hormonal cycle affects thermoregulation. Higher core temp in luteal phase. Pregnant women at higher risk
When to See a Doctor: Symptoms don't improve in 30 minutes or signs of heat stroke appear

Common Causes: Head impact during sports, falls, accidents
First Aid Steps: Stop activity, observe for confusion/dizziness, seek medical evaluation
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Loss of consciousness, severe headache, vomiting, slurred speech
Typical Recovery Time: 1-3 weeks with physical/cognitive rest; return-to-play protocol required
Male-Specific Notes: Higher incidence in contact sports. May return-to-play faster per old protocols
Female-Specific Notes: Longer recovery typical. Hormonal factors affect recovery. Postpartum mood effects
When to See a Doctor: Any suspected concussion needs medical evaluation; required before return to activity

Common Causes: Peanuts, shellfish, medications, insect stings, latex
First Aid Steps: Call 911, administer epinephrine auto-injector if available, lay person flat
Red Flag / Emergency Signs: Difficulty breathing, throat swelling, hives, anaphylaxis signs
Typical Recovery Time: Requires emergency hospital care; variable recovery
Male-Specific Notes: Similar presentation. Epinephrine dosing same weight-based
Female-Specific Notes: Pregnancy affects medication choices. Certain triggers more common (cosmetics, latex in medical settings)
When to See a Doctor: ALWAYS call 911 for severe allergic reactions; medical emergency
